source.title: LimiX: Unleashing Structured-Data Modeling Capability for Generalist Intelligence
source.authors: Xingxuan Zhang; Gang Ren; Han Yu; Hao Yuan; Hui Wang; Jiansheng Li; Jiayun Wu; Lang Mo; Li Mao; Mingchao Hao; Ningbo Dai; Renzhe Xu; Shuyang Li; Tianyang Zhang; Yue He; Yuanrui Wang; Yunjia Zhang; Zijing Xu; Dongzhe Li; Fang Gao; Hao Zou; Jiandong Liu; Jiashuo Liu; Jiawei Xu; Kaijie Cheng; Kehan Li; Linjun Zhou; Qing Li; Shaohua Fan; Xiaoyu Lin; Xinyan Han; Xuanyue Li; Yan Lu; Yuan Xue; Yuanyuan Jiang; Zimu Wang; Zhenlei Wang; Peng Cui

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equation formatting appears imperfect in the extracted text; equations below are recorded as shown.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests scaling relationships in structured-data models, a different setting from language-model pretraining, and reports results for dataset size, parameter count, and downstream metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results in Section 8. Comparisons to LLM scaling work in the introduction are context, not extracted results. No values from cited studies are included.
record.test_reason: Section 8 reports the study's own scaling fits for a new kind of system, tabular in-context foundation models (LimiX). It fits M = a·N^c + b for downstream loss and metrics on BCCO-CLS/REG against dataset size and parameter count. This is a new-setting result for V5, and for V6 in the structured-data setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors assume a priori that metrics follow M = a·N^c + b. They conclude that LDM loss and downstream metrics follow a predictable power law in data and parameters, 'analogous' to LLMs, with diminishing returns. They also say data and model scaling should be balanced. Their stated ranges (to 1e13 tokens and about 1B parameters) exceed the measured 1.7e12 tokens and 16.53M parameters; the larger figures are extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales structured-data models and evaluates downstream task losses and metrics, rather than measuring held-out language-model pretraining loss and compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.problems: The reported losses are downstream task losses, not held-out pretraining loss. Dataset-size fit results are given as an aggregate R2 > 0.99 rather than individual fits. The paper reports experimental parameter counts through 16.53M but describes fits extrapolated up to 1.6G; it does not report uncertainty intervals for fit parameters.

untested.parts: Not tested on language models. Pretraining loss is not measured, and no compute axis is used.
Fits are extrapolated to 1.6G parameters, but no larger run checks the extrapolation.
No shape or architecture sweep at a fixed parameter count.
Not tested: image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling, and spans of several orders of magnitude (only about 1.2 orders are tested).
Not tested: downstream performance against pretraining loss, and LM downstream tasks.
No comparison of fitting choices. Near-zero exponents are reported but not discussed as curvature.

missing.what: Per-model-size fitted constants and exponents for loss versus dataset size (only aggregate R2 > 0.99 is stated)
F1 fit equation versus parameter count (omitted because R2 < 0.9)
Inconsistent stated ranges: setup gives 1e11–1.7e12 tokens and up to 16.53M parameters, but conclusions say 1e11–1e13 tokens and about one billion parameters

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Evaluation was run without retrieval. No uncertainty is reported for the fits. Several exponents print as −0.000, which suggests a near-logarithmic or degenerate fit and weakens the power-law reading for the parameter axis. The domain is tabular models pretrained on synthetic SCM data, so V1–V4 do not apply directly.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss of language models against parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs.
It does not conduct fixed-compute-budget comparisons or measure a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
It does not test how architecture details such as depth and width affect loss at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling in structured-data models, but not image/video models, repeated-data training, or transfer and fine-tuning scaling laws. Its losses are downstream task losses, not held-out pretraining loss.
It tests downstream metrics against dataset size and parameter count for structured-data models, but not language-model downstream tasks or downstream performance against pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitting choices or setups to test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Tabular LDMs, downstream loss versus dataset size (1e11–1.7e12 tokens), 1.05M–16.53M parameters
relationships.reason: Loss falls with data for every model size, power-law fits have R2 > 0.99, and larger models reach lower loss (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased with data at every model size, power-law fits achieved R²>0.99, and larger models reached lower loss.

relationships.condition: Tabular LDMs, downstream loss versus parameter count (1.05M–16.53M)
relationships.reason: Fits reach R2 0.96–0.99, but the exponents are reported as −0.000 with large offsetting constants. This is a near-logarithmic fit over about 1 order of magnitude, not a clean power law (R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Fits reached R² = 0.96–0.99, but exponents reported as −0.000 and large offsetting constants produced nearly logarithmic behavior over about one decade of model size.

relationships.condition: Tabular LDMs on BCCO, AUC and ACC versus parameter count
relationships.reason: AUC and ACC rise with parameters, with power-law fits of R2 0.9044 and 0.9933 (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: AUC and accuracy increased with parameter count, with power-law fits achieving R² of 0.9044 and 0.9933, respectively.

relationships.condition: Tabular LDMs on BCCO, F1 and regression R2 score versus parameter count
relationships.reason: The F1 fit is weak (R2 0.68, no equation given). The regression R2-score fit has an exponent of −0.000, so it is not a clean power law (R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: The F1 scaling fit had R² = 0.68, while the regression R²-score fit had an essentially zero exponent of −0.000.
